## S7. WADE: the subset-aware differential-expression statistic {#sec-wade-method}

The discovery section reports what the contrasts found. This supplement carries
how the statistic works, why inference is by permutation with a tail
refinement, and — the part that matters most for reading the nominations — what
the method does *not* guarantee on a cohort this size.

### S7.1 Why not a t-test, Wilcoxon, or DESeq2

Standard differential-expression tests compare group *means* or *ranks* and
assume the two groups differ by a location shift. That assumption is wrong for
the question here. A cancer "case" group is heterogeneous by construction: a
gene elevated in 15 of 60 cases and silent in the other 45 has a modest mean
difference and an unremarkable rank-sum, yet a subtype marker is exactly what
this cohort is being mined for. A location-shift test is not merely
underpowered against that signal — it is testing a different hypothesis.

WADE's response is to compare the two groups' whole **distributions** and then
read the part of the comparison where a rare high-expressing subset would
appear.

### S7.2 The statistic

For each gene, WADE evaluates both groups' empirical quantile functions
$Q_{\text{case}}(p)$ and $Q_{\text{ctrl}}(p)$ on a shared grid of
$\min(n_0, n_1)$ probabilities — the smaller group's size, since that is the
resolution at which the two can be compared without interpolation carrying the
result. The signed area between them is

$$\texttt{diff.mean} \;=\; \int_0^1 \big[Q_{\text{case}}(p) - Q_{\text{ctrl}}(p)\big]\,dp \;=\; \mu_{\text{case}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}},$$

which is the ordinary mean difference — the **bulk** axis. The integral of the
*absolute* difference is the 1-Wasserstein distance $W_1$, reported as `w1`.

Because `diff.mean` collapses a rare-subset signal and a whole-group shift to
the same number, WADE adds two **shape** statistics read from the upper tail of
the quantile difference:

- **`tail.mean`** — the mean difference over the top-10% quantiles. This is the
  **subset** axis.
- **`tail.conc`** — the share of the total signed area falling in that tail, so
  a value near 1 marks a gene whose entire case-control difference is carried
  by its highest-expressing cases.

This joins two literatures. The quantile/Wasserstein
differential-distribution test (cf. scDD, waddR) supplies the mechanism;
cancer-outlier profile analysis (COPA, OS, ORT, MOST, LSOSS) supplies the
subset-detection goal.

Reading the two axes together is the point, and the per-gene diagnostic in the
main text is the intended way to do it: the cumulative signed area accumulates
left to right and its endpoint at $p = 1$ equals `diff.mean`, so a broad shift
rises steadily across all quantiles while a rare high subset stays flat and then
climbs inside the tail window.

### S7.3 Why permutation, and why a tail refinement

There is no tractable null distribution for a quantile-area statistic on
zero-inflated capture data, so inference is empirical: case/control labels are
shuffled and the statistic recomputed, `r WADE_NPERMS` times per contrast, on
both axes independently.

Two details matter for reproducibility.

**The noise draw is held out of the null.** WADE applies a small uniform
continuity jitter once, at count precision with a fixed seed, to break ties in
sparse data — then permutes labels on that *fixed* normalized matrix. Inference
is therefore conditional on the jitter rather than integrating over it, which is
what makes a given seed reproduce a given result exactly.

**The empirical p has a floor, and the floor is not the answer.** With $B$
permutations the smallest empirical p-value is $1/(B+1)$, and a gene whose
observed statistic exceeds every permuted value is only known to be "below that".
WADE refines such cases by fitting a Generalized Pareto distribution to the
upper tail of the permutation null (Knijnenburg et al. 2009, method-of-moments —
closed-form and dependency-free) and reading p from its CDF.

Three deliberate choices inside that refinement are worth stating, because each
prevents a specific failure:

1. **The $\xi \le 0$ branch.** When the moment fit returns a non-positive shape
   — a light or bounded tail — the GPD has a hard upper bound at $-\sigma/\xi$
   and a strong observed statistic collapses to a machine-epsilon p-value. WADE
   uses the $\xi \to 0$ exponential limit instead, which is well-defined for all
   $y \ge 0$ and appropriately conservative.
2. **A resolution floor at $1/(B \cdot n_{\text{tail}})$.** With
   `r WADE_NPERMS` permutations and 250 tail points, the smallest defensible
   tail probability is about `r sprintf("%.1e", 1/(WADE_NPERMS*250))`.
   Returning anything smaller would be a fiction, and worse, a degenerate bound
   collapsing to machine epsilon creates false ties that *mis-order* the
   strongest hits — the one thing rank-based nomination cannot tolerate.
3. **Refinement is applied only where it is needed** — genes with fewer than 10
   exceedances — so a well-resolved p-value is never replaced by an extrapolated
   one.

### S7.4 What the permutation test is actually protecting against here

On this cohort the p-values are **not** the discovery product, and it is worth
being precise about what they are for.

Exactly one gene across all `r wade_n_runs` runs reaches FDR < 0.10 on either
axis, and the callout below shows why it should not be read as a discovery. That
is a **power** statement about group sizes, not evidence of no signal — the
enrichment of nominal *p* < 0.01 genes over chance expectation in the main text
is the counter-evidence. Nomination is therefore by **rank score**: a signed
rank-product rewarding genes high in cases, low in controls, and large in
fold-change (`score`), plus a subset-aware variant that substitutes the tail
statistic for fold-change (`tail.score`). Both are in $[-1, 1]$ and both are
*heuristics* — they are the lab's panel-selection score, not an inferential
quantity, and a rank of 1 is not a claim of significance.

What the permutation p-value still does, indispensably, is **refuse
single-outlier genes**. A gene driven by one extreme sample can post a large
`diff.mean` and a `tail.conc` near 1 — it looks exactly like a subset marker on
the shape statistics alone — but no shuffled null can be beaten by one sample,
so the permutation test declines it. The shape statistics *describe* subset
structure; the permutation p-value is what stops a single outlier being called a
discovery. That is why the nomination tables carry it even though it gates
nothing.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The one FDR-significant result in this section is an extrapolation artefact

Across all `r wade_n_runs` contrast runs (both cohorts), exactly **one** gene
reaches FDR < 0.10 on either axis: **`r wade_gpd_gene`** on the subset axis of
the pancreatic-precursor contrast, at padj = `r sprintf("%.4f", wade_gpd_padj)`.
It should not be read as a discovery, for three reasons that compound.

Its p-value is `r sprintf("%.0e", wade_gpd_p)`, which is **exactly the GPD
extrapolation floor** $1/(B \cdot n_{\text{tail}})$ — not a measured
exceedance rate. The empirical permutation p-value cannot go below
$1/(B+1) = `r sprintf("%.4f", 1/(WADE_NPERMS+1))`$, and at that value BH across
`r format(wade_gpd_ngenes, big.mark = ",")` genes gives padj ≈
`r sprintf("%.1f", wade_gpd_padj_emp)` — nowhere near significance. **The entire
result is produced by the tail fit**, and it is the only gene in the section
whose p-value sits at that floor.

The contrast it comes from has `r wade_gpd_nprobs` in the smaller group, so its
tail window is a **single order statistic** — the screen already marks it
`descriptive` for this reason.

And the signal is carried by `r wade_gpd_npat` patients
(`r wade_gpd_nlib` libraries above the control maximum), which is below the
combinatorial floor described next.

This is not an argument against the tail refinement, which is doing what it was
designed to do: extrapolate where the empirical resolution runs out, and floor
the answer honestly rather than returning machine epsilon. It is an argument for
reading *any* p-value at the floor as "beyond this cohort's resolution" rather
than as a small number. The refinement extends resolution; it does not
manufacture power.
:::

There is a hard limit underneath this, and it is combinatorial rather than
statistical. If $k$ samples carry a signal, the probability that label
shuffling puts all $k$ in the case group is
$\binom{n_1}{k}/\binom{n_1+n_0}{k}$ — for the primary contrast that is
`r sprintf("%.2f", wade_floor_tbl$k2[wade_floor_tbl$id == WADE_PRIMARY])` at
$k=2$ and
`r sprintf("%.2f", wade_floor_tbl$k3[wade_floor_tbl$id == WADE_PRIMARY])` at
$k=3$. Below roughly 5% of cases, a shuffled null reproduces the signal and
**no permutation test can separate it**, whatever the effect size. That floor,
not the FDR threshold, is the real limit on subtype discovery in this cohort.

### S7.5 The quantile grid is a sample-size constraint, not a parameter

Because the grid has $\min(n_0, n_1)$ points and the tail window is the top 10%
of them, the subset axis needs enough order statistics to exist:

| smaller group | grid points | tail window | subset axis |
|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| 5 | 5 | 1 | a single order statistic — not a subset detector |
| 10 | 10 | 1 | still one point |
| 20 | 20 | 2 | minimum for a tail *mean* |
| 34 | 34 | 4 | usable |

This is why the contrast screen reports `k_tail` and why contrasts below 20 in
the smaller group nominate on the bulk axis only. It is also why the three
control-vs-control comparisons are marked `descriptive`: their effect sizes are
real measurements, but a one-point "tail mean" is an order statistic wearing the
name of an average, and reporting it as subset detection would be the analysis
overstating its own resolution.

### S7.6 What WADE does not do

Stated plainly, because each of these is a live limitation on the results in the
main text rather than a hypothetical:

- **No covariate adjustment.** WADE is a two-group test. There is no panel term,
  no depth term, no patient random effect. A confound can therefore be
  *detected* (the contrast screen) but not *removed* — which is why a
  design-confounded contrast is refused rather than corrected, and why
  panel-matching is done by restricting the libraries instead.
- **No repeated-measures handling.** Libraries from the same patient are treated
  as independent, and they are not. The screen reports every statistic at both
  the library and one-library-per-patient unit for this reason, and the
  patient-level unit is the one that decides feasibility.
- **Its own normalization.** `wade()` applies a (count, normalizer) TPM-like
  scaling internally rather than consuming the project's `ic_spl_sum`
  normalized matrix. Measured on this cohort the two correct depth comparably —
  residual Spearman of per-library mean abundance against on-target spliced
  yield is `r sprintf("%.2f", wade_norm_rho$wade_full)` for WADE's internal TPM
  against `r sprintf("%.2f", wade_norm_rho$proj_full)` for `ic_spl_sum`, both
  against `r sprintf("%.2f", wade_norm_rho$raw_full)` uncorrected — so this is
  a redundancy rather than a defect. It is nonetheless a second normalization
  decision living inside a test, and the standalone-package plan moves it out
  (see `WADE_REPO_SCOPE.md`).
- **Directionality.** The nomination scores reward up-in-case genes. Genes
  *lost* in cases are visible in `diff.mean` but are not what the ranking
  surfaces.

### S7.7 Implementation and cost

The statistic is `cfrna_analysis/wade.R`, a self-contained module with no
knowledge of this cohort, its diseases, or its probe panels — written as the
prototype for a standalone package. The cfRNA-specific layer (the contrast
registry, the confounding screen, cohort plumbing, caching) is
`R/wade_contrasts.R`, and the control taxonomy is `R/control_strata.R`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wade-cost
wade_cost |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrr",
    caption = paste("Compute cost per contrast at", WADE_NPERMS,
      "label permutations with GPD tail refinement on both axes.",
      "Results are cached to `cfrna_analysis/cache/wade/` keyed on the contrast,",
      "the cohort name and fingerprint, the gene count, both groups' library",
      "ids, and the permutation settings -- so a re-render reloads rather than",
      "recomputes, and a store refresh or a library moving between groups",
      "invalidates the entry rather than silently reusing it."))
```
